# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: *A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration* (Varden County)

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot, and it fixes most of what I criticised there:
- **Comparison group:** offices were randomised to treatment or control.
- **Output:** taken from administrative records, not manager ratings.
- **Hours:** actual hours from timesheets, not scheduled hours.
- **Pre-specification:** a registered protocol, with strata defined before randomisation.
- **Exploratory work:** clearly labelled as such.

The authors' own point that scheduled-hours denominators inflate per-hour gains (22% vs 12.5%) directly confirms the concern I raised about the pilot.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Actual hours fell by 12.9% and 17.0%.
- Per-hour gains follow from the per-FTE and hours figures: 0.979/0.871 = +12.5%, and 0.886/0.830 = +6.7%.
- On a scheduled-hours basis, case-processing would show +22.4%.

The remaining issues are mostly about inference with few clusters, missing outcomes, and cost. A few of them could change how the results read.

---

## 1. Inference with 10–14 clusters

- **The problem.** Standard cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward when there are few clusters. Here there are 14 clusters in case-processing and only 10 in the counter stratum, so the reported CIs are probably too narrow.
- **What to report.** The paper should state the correction used, for example:
  - CR2 / Bell–McCaffrey standard errors,
  - wild cluster bootstrap, or
  - randomisation inference, which is natural for a randomised design.
- **Why it matters.**
  - The counter-stratum per-hour CI (+0.4 to +13.3) barely excludes zero. With a proper small-sample correction it may not.
  - The per-FTE fall in counter offices (−16.9 to −5.9) is likely robust.
- **Derived estimates.** It is unclear how the CIs for output per actual hour were constructed, given that the hours reductions themselves are reported without uncertainty.

## 2. Outcomes that are missing or analysed inconsistently

| Outcome | Problem |
|---|---|
| Waiting time (4.2 → 6.9 min) | Reported for treated offices only, before vs after. Not a difference-in-differences estimate, despite being a registered secondary outcome. |
| Abandoned calls (6% → 10%) | Same issue: treated offices only, no control comparison. |
| Quality (3.1% v 3.0%; 11.8% v 10.9%) | Raw treated-vs-control levels, not DiD, and no CIs. The counter quality result (repeat contacts up about 0.9 points) isn't discussed in the text. |
| Sick days (−29%) | Pooled across strata, with no CI and no stratum-specific estimates. |
| Resignations (3.9% v 7.4%) | Raw comparison, no CI. The authors correctly call it imprecise. |
| Case-processing backlog and time to decision | Not reported. This is the key quality risk for queue-based work. Clearing cases "at any point within statutory deadlines" means slower processing and deadline breaches wouldn't show up in cases closed. The Limitations section flags backlog build-up, but the county's case-management system should already hold this data. |

**Appeal lag.** Appeals take time to be lodged and decided. Overturn rates at nine months will under-capture decisions made late in the trial.

## 3. A possible inconsistency in the counter results

- **The figures don't obviously add up.** If public demand was unchanged, an 11.4% fall in contacts handled per employee means about 11% fewer contacts served overall. Yet abandoned calls rose only 4 points, which on its own implies roughly a 4% fall in handled calls (0.90/0.94).
- **Explanations the paper should address:**
  - members of the public giving up before contacting the office at all,
  - a shift to other channels or other offices,
  - differing trends in control offices, or
  - a change in demand.
- **Repeat contacts cut the other way.** They count as "contacts handled." A rise in repeat contacts therefore inflates measured output while reflecting worse service. So the true service loss may be somewhat larger than −11.4%.

## 4. Spillovers between treated and control offices

- **The risk.** Randomising by office prevents contamination between colleagues, but not displacement of demand.
  - Callers who abandon calls, or visitors facing longer waits, may be routed or choose to go to control offices.
  - That would raise control output and exaggerate the treated–control gap in counter offices.
- **Check.** Do telephone lines share a routing system or overflow queues? Are counter offices substitutable for the public?
- **Possible cross-stratum link.** If counters feed cases into case-processing offices, a change in counter throughput could affect case inflow.

## 5. Mechanism in counter offices

- **The per-hour gain there is probably mostly higher utilisation, not efficiency.** With fewer staff present during unchanged opening hours, each staff member has less idle time between customers. So output per hour rises even if nobody works any faster.
- **The authors' framing is correct but could be sharper.** They say "gains per hour do not by themselves imply the hours reduction pays for itself." In coverage-bound work, the per-hour metric partly measures the same understaffing that produced the longer waits.
- **The design tests one policy, not every way of implementing it.** It covers fewer hours with unchanged staffing. It does not cover a reduction with backfill hiring, which is how coverage-bound employers would likely implement a shorter week. State this explicitly.

## 6. Cost is missing from the analysis

- **Overtime makes case-processing more expensive.** Treated case-processing staff averaged 33.0 actual hours against 30 scheduled, and timesheets "include any overtime claimed."
  - If those roughly 3 hours a week are paid overtime, then full pay plus premium-rate overtime for roughly the same output (−2.1%) means cost per case rose.
  - Output per hour is not the same thing as output per unit of labour cost.
- **Report cost per output** (cases closed, or contacts handled) alongside the productivity measures. This bears directly on the county's stated question about extending the schedule "without loss of service."
- **Unclaimed hours.** Timesheets capture claimed overtime only. Unrecorded work (checking email on the day off, unclaimed extra time) would make actual hours higher, and the true per-hour gain smaller, than reported.

## 7. Pre-registration details to make explicit

- **Pooled vs stratum results.** Was the registered primary analysis by stratum, or pooled? If pooled, report the pooled estimate alongside the stratum results. Since stratification preceded randomisation, by-stratum analysis was probably planned, but say so.
- **Weighting.** State whether estimates are weighted by office or by staff, and report staff numbers per stratum and arm.

## 8. The exploratory meetings analysis

The authors handle this appropriately: they flag it as unregistered, note it rests on seven offices, decline to infer causation, and have pre-registered a confirmatory test. Two additions would help:
- **No baseline.** Meeting data come from month six only. The 3.8 vs 7.1 hours gap could partly reflect pre-existing differences, which is plausible with only 7 offices per arm. Pre-period calendar data, if retrievable, would settle this.
- **Confounding in the correlation.** The r = 0.71 across treated offices may reflect manager engagement in general, not meeting reduction specifically.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Treatment awareness.** The "John Henry" effect (control staff working harder because they know a trial is running) is acknowledged. Pre-period trends in control offices could help show whether it occurred.
- **Summary wording.** The Summary reports sick days (−29%) without a CI, alongside estimates that have them. Add the interval, or note that it's pooled and less precise.

---

## Highest-value revisions

1. Apply a small-cluster correction (or randomisation inference) to all CIs.
2. Report waiting times, abandoned calls, quality and sick days as DiD estimates with CIs, and by stratum.
3. Add case-processing backlog and time-to-decision outcomes.
4. Report cost per output, accounting for overtime pay.
5. Reconcile the counter output fall (−11.4%) with the abandonment rise (+4 points), and assess displacement to control offices.
6. Clarify the pre-registration (stratum vs pooled) and the weighting.

Overall, the central conclusions are well supported by this design and appropriately hedged:
- in queue-based work, little loss of output per employee;
- in coverage-bound work, a real loss of output and service;
- scheduled-hours denominators overstate per-hour gains.

The main risk is that, without the cost and backlog data, the case-processing result looks more favourable than it may be.
